Trail: Accurate Local Smart Home Control Using Decision Models

 

Maleeha Masood 1  Deepak Vasisht 1  Indranil Gupta 1 

††footnotetext: 1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Correspondence to: Maleeha Masood <maleeha2@illinois.edu>.
Proceedings of the 8t​h\mathit{8}^{th} MLSys Conference, Santa Clara, CA, USA, 2025. Copyright 2025 by the author(s).
Abstract

Natural-language driven smart home control remains challenging: cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) raise privacy concerns, while local Small Language Models (SLMs) can generate invalid actions or misinterpret requests. We introduce Trail (Typed Registry-Anchored Inference for Language commands in Smart Homes), a fully local framework that replaces open-ended command generation with hierarchical typed decisions. Trail exploits the natural structure of a home’s action space, selecting a room, device, and operation from candidates derived from the runtime device registry. This ensures valid actions while enabling confidence-based abstention when requests cannot be reliably resolved. We also design a structured memory module that uses typed decisions to support user preferences, device references, and multi-turn interactions. To evaluate Trail, we extend HomeBench Li et al. (2025) and generate three datasets: Trek-Base, which tests natural-language variation; Trek-Robust, which evaluates robustness to changes in the home and its description; and Trek-Memory, which assesses conversational memory across multi-turn interactions. Trail achieves 85.3% accuracy on Trek-Robust versus 69.8% for a finetuned Qwen3.5-4B baseline, while remaining competitive on Trek-Base requests. With memory, Trail resolves 75.6% of the requests that depend on earlier turns, compared with 42.5% for the finetuned baseline given conversation history.

1 Introduction

Adapting smart homes to user preferences has been a longstanding research area Mozer (1998); Rashidi and Cook (2009); King et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2026); Lim et al. (2026); iFLYTEK Open Source (2026). With recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), natural-language interfaces allow for more conversational smart home control. Accurately interpreting such requests is especially important because incorrect actions have physical consequences such as leaving an oven running unattended or unlocking the front door at night. Today, the interpretation of user requests often relies on cloud-hosted LLMs, requiring private user data to be sent to third parties for inference and risking service disruptions during network outages. Small Language Models (SLMs) offer a promising alternative through local inference, but they struggle with complex tasks and generalization Caballar and Stryker (2026).

We present Trail – Typed Registry-Anchored Inference for Language commands in Smart Homes – an entirely local smart home control framework that is accurate, completely private, and is always available. Trail leverages the new generation of Decision Models (aka System One models), such as Jev Almeida (2026) and Microsoft-Decision-1 Srivastava (2026). Unlike traditional language models that generate free-form text, Decision Models score predefined choices and return their associated confidence scores. Their non-generative inference enables fast, structured decision-making, making them promising for interactive local smart home control.

Trail formulates smart home control as a selection problem using typed decisions. Each typed decision presents a question and a set of predefined choices, which a Decision Model scores and selects from. At runtime, these choices are derived from a home’s device registry, which defines the available devices, their supported operations, and their parameter constraints. This allows Trail to adapt to new devices without retraining and refuse requests that cannot be reliably resolved, rather than guessing — such a capability of “I don’t know how to do it” is a missing feature from today’s LLMs, which do not stop trying even when the task is impossible. Furthermore, Trail runs entirely locally, preserving user privacy and availability. In designing Trail, we make the following key contributions.

Smart Home Control as Hierarchical Decisions. Our key insight is that a smart home’s action space has a natural hierarchical structure: resolving a user request involves first identifying the relevant room, then selecting a device within that room, and finally determining the operation to perform on that device. For example, given the request “dim the living room light to 40%”, Trail first selects the living room, then the light within that room, and finally the brightness operation of the selected light. Each decision considers only the candidates consistent with previous selections, reducing the number of choices the model must evaluate at each step.

Integrating User Preferences and References. We design a structured memory module that allows Trail to remember and recall user preferences and references. (1) Preferences store a preferred value for a device’s setting, optionally tied to a situation (e.g., reading-lamp brightness 40 when reading). (2) References map a user’s own words to a device (e.g., “the front light” to foyer.light), including the device a user has just operated so that “turn it off” can refer back to it. Memory is managed using typed decisions: they decide what to store, link each stored record to a device in the home’s registry, and retrieve the relevant records when a later request needs them. This enables personalized, context-aware control without placing conversation history in the SLM’s prompt.

New Smart Home Datasets. To address the paucity of natural-language datasets for smart homes, we extend HomeBench Li et al. (2025) to generate 3 smart home datasets. First, we introduce Trek-Base, which tests natural-language variations in user requests, including implicit device references and goal-oriented commands. Second, we develop Trek-Robust, a stress test that evaluates robustness to changes in the home and its description. Third, we build Trek-Memory, that converts Trek-Base into 100 multi-turn conversations, one per home, with device states that carry over between turns and inserted requests that require memory, such as user-defined device nicknames and corrections.

We implement Trail using JevK5 Serikbay (2026), an open-source Decision Model built on Qwen3.5-4B. We evaluate Trail on Trek-Base, Trek-Robust and Trek-Memory against direct-generation, retrieval, agentic and slot-filling baselines. Trail stays within 4 points of the strongest baseline on Trek-Base, makes 2.1×\times fewer errors on Trek-Robust, and resolves 2.1×\times more of the requests that require memory.

2 Background: Decision Models and Typed Decisions

Decision Models Almeida (2026); Deußer et al. (2026); Rafe and Das (2026); Sharma et al. (2026) are non-generative LLMs that make fast, structured decisions over predefined outputs using typed decisions. Instead of generating output tokens, a Decision Model scores the candidates of the typed decision and returns the choices with their associated confidence score.

A typed decision restricts the model’s output to a predefined type and set of valid choices, such as selecting a device from those available in a home. For example, given the user command “Turn on the kitchen lights”, a smart home controller can define a typed decision over the set of available devices, such as light, switch, coffee maker, fridge. The model scores these candidates and selects light, rather than generating a free-formed device name. This ensures that the selected device belongs to the set of valid options.

Decision Models are particularly well suited to smart home control, where the available devices are known, but may vary across homes and change over time. Typed decisions allow the model to select from these at runtime. Trail uses JevK5 Serikbay (2026) to provide this typed decision interface. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to use Decision Models for local smart home control.

3 Motivation

We describe two failures in local smart home control: invalid actions and incorrect interpretation of user requests. These failures motivate a design that separates semantic interpretation of the user requests from runtime enforcement of action constraints and supports abstention when a request cannot be resolved from the available context.

Example Setup. Consider a smart home with four devices: a) light bulb in the living room, b) thermostat in the living room, c) light bulb on the balcony, and d) a lock on the front door. Each light bulb can be turned on or off, and configured to a brightness level 0–100. The thermostat can be set to 16–30∘C, and the front door can be locked or unlocked. We use Qwen2.5 1.5B, 3B and 7B to translate user requests to device actions within this home – Table 1 shows the requests and outputs that we refer to in this section.

Failure Type 1: Invalid Action Failures. Consider request – the 7B model generates bedroom.AC.on(), which is a reasonable output if the smart home contained the device. Similarly, request specifies an invalid brightness level – the 1.5B model generates balcony.light.set_brightness(150), placing the invalid value into the actuation command. The 3B model makes an additional mistake by introducing a syntax error (: instead of . after light).

These failures show that SLMs do not consistently enforce device capabilities, argument bounds, or command syntax. Such constraints should instead be enforced by the runtime.

Failure Type 2: Interpretation Failures. A valid output can still misinterpret a user’s request. The request is ambiguous because the example home contains two light bulbs. All SLMs turned off the living room light, despite insufficient information to determine that this is the user’s intended target. Similarly, request requires interpreting how much to increase the temperature based on the current state and user preferences.

Unlike invalid actuations, these failures cannot be prevented by enforcing device constraints alone. The model must resolve the user’s intent from the available context or abstain when the request remains ambiguous.

Failure Amplifiers. These failure modes are further exacerbated by i) compound requests, which contain more than one command in the same user request (for e.g., ), and ii) convoluted natural-language expressions like slang expressions e.g. ‘‘the heat has me cooked’’ which means the user wants to lower the temperature, not actually cook.

Implication. These failures are particularly consequential in smart homes, where incorrect commands can affect physical devices. For request , all SLMs generate invalid commands that could leave the front door unlocked (possibly even at night). While not unique to SLMs, such failures highlight the limitations of relying on unconstrained command generation for reliable smart home control.

4 Trail’s Design

Trail translates natural-language requests into executable smart home API calls through a hierarchy of typed decisions grounded in the home’s device registry. This section describes its design, summarized in Algorithm 1. More details about the typed decisions used in Trail are in Appendix 10.2.

4.1 Smart Home Control Problem

Trail formulates smart home control as a selection problem where a smart home system selects actions to satisfy a user’s request. The space of possible actions is large – a naive selection considers R​D​ORDO candidates for a home with RR rooms, DD devices per room, and OO operations per device, and may produce invalid device calls. This action space also varies across homes and changes as devices are added or removed. In contrast, Trail considers only R+D+OR+D+O candidates while ensuring that the selected device and operation are valid.

We define a smart home HH by its device registry RHR_{H} and device state SHS_{H}. RHR_{H} defines HH’s closed set of available o​p​e​r​a​t​i​o​n​soperations and their parameter signatures. SHS_{H} records each device’s current status and attributes. Fig. 1 shows an example RHR_{H} and accompanying SHS_{H}. Let AHA_{H} denote the set of valid calls to these operations with arguments in their declared domains.

Given a user request uu, that may contain several requests ss (for e.g., “dim the balcony light to 50% and make it 2 degrees cooler”), smart home control maps uu, RHR_{H}, and SHS_{H} to an ordered list of actions in AHA_{H} or refusals. The refusal is required when the home cannot do what was asked, when the request does not say enough to act, or when the request asks for a value the device cannot take. The correct output is a list with one item per single request.

4.2 System Design

Hierarchical Action Resolution. Trail needs to convert each natural language request into a structured query. To do so, Trail organises RHR_{H} as a tree. Each registry entry in RHR_{H} has a dotted name room.device.operation(arguments) and a signature that lists its parameters with their types, for e.g., hall.heat.set_temp(temp:int). In the tree, each room branches into its devices, and each device branches into its supported operations. Selecting a room narrows the candidate devices, and selecting a device narrows the available operations. A path from the root to a leaf therefore identifies an executable operation in the home.

The three questions that Trail asks to resolve all user requests are: (i) Which room does this command refer to? (ii) Which device in that room does this command control? and (iii) Which operation on that device does this command ask for? Consider the request “dim the living room light to 40%”. At the root, Trail asks which room the request refers to, offering the rooms in the registry as choices. Selecting living_room exposes only the devices in that room. Whole-home devices, such as a vacuum robot, are offered as choices within every room. The next question identifies light, whose available operations then become the choices for the final question. Selecting set_brightness completes the path.

As its selector for each level, Trail deploys a singular instance of JevK5 Serikbay (2026); Almeida (2026), an open-sourced Decision Model finetuned to hierarchical smart home questions . The selector grounds each request in the registry through typed decisions: each decision selects from a predefined set of options corresponding to rooms, devices, or operations. At each of the three levels, the selector sees the original request, the selections made so far, and the current node’s children – it never needs to consider all RHR_{H} actions in a single decision. The selector returns a probability distribution over the options, which Trail uses both to select the next branch and to accumulate confidence in the resulting action path. This path selection occurs independently for each sub-command ss in the user request uu.

Deciding When to Accept or Refuse. Restricting choices to the registry prevents invalid operations (Failure Type 1, §3) but does not guarantee that the selected action matches the user’s intent (Failure Type 2). Unlike LLMs that may persist even when a task is impossible, Trail can recognize when to give up. To enable this, each hierarchical typed decision includes a none option, allowing the selector to assign probability to the possibility that no available choice matches.

Trail continues through the highest-probability real option, retaining its probability without renormalising away none, even when none scores higher. It accumulates confidence along the path: c⁡(s)=p⁡(r∣s)​p​(d∣s,r)​p​(o∣s,r,d)c(s)=p(r\mid s)p(d\mid s,r)p(o\mid s,r,d), where rr, dd, and oo are the selected room, device, and operation, respectively, and pp is the probability assigned by the selector given the request and preceding selections.

After all three hierarchical decisions and reaching an operation, Trail refuses if c⁡(s)<τc(s)<\tau; otherwise, it proceeds to resolve the operation’s arguments. This defers the refusal decision until the complete path has been evaluated, ensuring that one uncertain level doesn’t decide if the user request can be resolved or not.

Argument Resolution. Selecting a device and operation is not sufficient to execute commands that require parameters, such as setting a temperature or brightness level. Trail must also determine the intended value while ensuring it satisfies the device’s constraints. To do so, Trail uses the operation’s parameter name and type from the registry and its allowed range from the device state.

If the final action takes no parameter (for e.g., living_room.light.turn_on()), the request resolution is complete. However, when uu states a numeric target, Trail parses it directly. Relative changes are computed directly using the current value in SHS_{H} – “2 degrees cooler” becomes 21−2=1921-2=19 when the current temperature is 21∘21^{\circ}C. When uu leaves the value unspecified, as in “make it a bit warmer”, Trail uses a coarse-to-fine selection procedure. For an integer domain [ℓ,h][\ell,h], it first offers the selector a coarse set of evenly spaced candidate values. After each selection, Trail narrows the interval around the selected value to resolve the argument. All candidates are restricted to the declared domain and an out-of-range value produces a refusal. Finally, for enumerated parameters such as operating modes, the selector instead chooses directly among the declared options.

4.3 Memory Module

Natural-language requests often rely on user-specific context that cannot be inferred from the request or the home’s current state. For example, “turn off the front light” requires knowing which device the user calls the “front light,” while “set the lights to my usual brightness” requires knowing the user’s preferred setting. To capture these two types of information, Trail maintains a structured memory of preferences and references, stored separately for each user in a household.

Preferences associate device operations with preferred values, optionally conditioned on a situation, e.g., setting the living-room light to 40% when reading or the dehumidifier to 100% when it rains. References map user-defined names like “the front light” to devices and track recently operated devices, enabling follow-up requests such as “turn it off.”

This design integrates naturally with hierarchical action resolution: references identify the intended device before operation selection, while preferences supply missing values afterward. Memories are stored locally in a SQLite database.

Routing. For each sub-command ss, Trail first uses a typed decision to determine whether the user is requesting an immediate action, providing information to remember, or revising stored information or a previous action. The decision returns a probability distribution over three choices: now, remember, and revise. Since both remember and revise require memory processing, Trail routes the sub-command to the write path when 1−P⁡(now∣s)≥τm1-P(\texttt{now}\mid s)\geq\tau_{m}.

Writing Memory. For sub-commands routed to memory, a second typed decision identifies one of four operations: preference, alias, forget, or correction. Note that alias and correction both create references, while forget removes references or preferences. A preference stores a preferred value for a device operation (“I prefer the bedroom light at 40%”); a reference names a device (“call the hallway light the front light”); a forget request removes stored aliases or preferences; and a correction, when the previous action targeted the wrong device, re-runs that command on the intended device and remembers the user’s phrase for it.

Each memory operation uses Trail’s hierarchical action resolution to identify the relevant device. Typed decisions then select the information to store from candidate phrases drawn directly from the user’s message. For a preference, Trail takes the operation from this resolution, parses the preferred value from the message, e.g., brightness at 40%, and identifies any situational context by selecting relevant phrases from the message. For an alias, it selects the user-defined device name. For a correction, it selects the device reference in the earlier request, associates it with the corrected device, and re-executes the request. A forget operation removes the references the message mentions, or else the preferences of the identified device, from active memory. If the required information cannot be identified, Trail requests clarification without updating memory.

Reading Memory. When the command is not a memory write, Trail reads memory before and after the hierarchical action resolution. Consider a user who earlier said “call the hallway light the front light” and “I like the bedroom light at 40% when I’m reading”.

Before resolution, memory can fix the device. For “turn on the front light”, the saved name “front light” appears in the message, so the device is fixed to hallway.light and only the operation is chosen (turn_on): one typed decision instead of three. For a follow-up “now turn it off”, no saved name appears and no device is named, but the message refers back (“it”), so one typed decision chooses among the devices acted on in the last three turns, or “none of these”. A device named in the message is never overridden: with no matching name and no reference back, resolution runs over the whole home exactly as without memory.

After resolution, memory can supply the value. For “set the bedroom light to my usual, I’m reading”, the resolution selects bedroom.light.set_brightness but the message states no value. Trail looks up the saved preferences for that device and operation, finds the one whose situation (“reading”) appears in the message, and fills in 40. A value stated in the message (“to 60%”, “a bit brighter”) always takes precedence over a preference.

Finally, the action is checked against the home’s registry, the user’s permissions and the device’s allowed values, and is refused if any check fails; if saved names for several devices match, Trail asks the user which one is meant.

5 Training and Calibrating Trail

Trail’s design (§4) relies on a selector that answers its typed questions and on three values that control its behavior: a softmax temperature TT for the selector’s probabilities, the refusal threshold τ\tau, and the memory gate threshold τm\tau_{m}. This section describes the data used to obtain them.

5.1 Adapting HomeBench

To train (and later, evaluate) Trail to translate natural-language requests into valid device actions across diverse smart homes, we adapt HomeBench Li et al. (2025). HomeBench pairs user requests with executable device calls across 100 simulated homes, each exposing approximately 140 actions through its device registry. Each request uu contains up to ten sub-commands ss, each mapped to a device call or error_input if the home cannot execute it.

HomeBench’s requests are almost always explicit: they name the room, the device, the operation and the target value, as in “Lower the temperature of the air conditioner in the master bedroom to 20 degrees.” Such requests mainly test whether a system can map a fully specified instruction to an API call. In everyday requests, users may leave these details implicit: “make the master bedroom cooler”. We therefore use GPT-5 to rewrite HomeBench’s requests into four styles.

  • Original: the original HomeBench request (22.5%)

  • Explicit: colloquial but fully specified (22.5%)

  • Implied Device: device inferred from context (45%)

  • Goal Only: desired outcome, not action (10%)

The resulting corpus contains natural-language requests paired with action or refusal labels. Note that we do not make any changes to the home configurations or the ground truth provided. We drop rows where the ground truth was incorrect (undefined action or out-of-range values). The prompts used are provided in Appendix 10.3.

5.2 Selector Finetuning

Trail uses a finetuned selector for all of its typed decisions: the three levels of action resolution, argument selection, and memory operations. We finetune JevK5 Serikbay (2026) once, on action-resolution and argument decisions only, and reuse it for memory decisions without further training. Because the registry and the memory supply the options of every question at runtime, the finetuned selector needs no further training for a new home.

Constructing Decision Examples. Since Trail’s selector must answer hierarchical questions rather than generate complete device calls, we finetune it on individual typed decisions derived from the adapted HomeBench. We turn each labeled request into the individual choices the selector makes during inference. For example, an action labeled living_room.light.set_brightness(40) provides at least three examples: selecting the living room, selecting its light, and selecting the brightness operation. Each example pairs the request and the correct preceding selections with a question, the available options, and the correct answer. The user request stays the same.

For refusal requests, we label the first unmatched decision as none; for example, “turn on the living room fan” receives living_room for the room decision and none for the device decision if no fan exists. Actions with arguments provide additional examples. For an enumerated argument, the correct answer is the labeled option. For a numeric argument, the coarse selection targets the candidate closest to the labeled value, splitting the target probability equally if two candidates tie. The fine selection then targets the exact labeled integer among the nearby values.

Dataset Composition. The decision examples yield about 250,000 unique examples. We sample 100,000 decisions from this pool, allocating 25,000 each to room, device, operation, and argument selection. At each hierarchy level, refusal examples occupy up to half the budget, with positive examples filling the remainder. Within the argument category, enumerated, coarse, and refinement examples are sampled in proportion to their availability.

Training Configuration. We initialise the selector from JevK5, a Qwen3.5-4B checkpoint trained for typed decisions. We finetune it for one epoch using rank-16 LoRA, a learning rate of 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, 20 warm-up steps, and an 8,192-token batch budget per GPU across four GPUs.

5.3 Calibrating the Selector

Trail uses the selector’s probabilities to determine when to abstain, making calibration important for reliable refusal decisions. We apply temperature scaling, which adjusts confidence without changing the selected option. We fit T=1.0T=1.0 by minimizing negative log-likelihood on half of approximately 7,000 held-out decisions spanning room, device, operation, refusal, and value questions, and evaluate it on the remaining half.

Setting the Refusal Threshold. Trail refuses a sub-command when its path confidence c⁡(s)c(s) is below τ\tau. We use validation requests to set τ=0.27\tau=0.27.

Setting the Memory Gate. A typed decision sends memory statements to the write path using τm\tau_{m}. We use validation requests to set τm=0.74\tau_{m}=0.74 .

6 Evaluation Datasets

We build 3 smart home datasets for evaluating Trail.

6.1 Trek-Base: Test Set

We evaluate Trail on the test split of the adapted HomeBench (§5.1). The test set contains 15,476 requests over 100 homes. The split mixes single requests that the home supports (5,732), single requests for a device the home does not have (4,063) or an attribute the device does not have (2,523), and 3,158 utterances that combine 2 to 10 requests. We drop requests with inconsistent ground truths, leaving 14,166 valid requests. Because HomeBench’s train and test splits share homes and sentence templates, this dataset measures performance on familiar homes and familiar phrasing.

6.2 Trek-Robust: Robustness Evaluation

Trek-Robust tests whether a system still works when the home or the wording changes. We introduce 9 categories that change either the user request or the home: counterfactual – the same user request in two slightly different homes so that the correct answers differ, unseen capability – the device lacks the requested operation, has a new operation signature, or does not declare what it can do, missing information – the needed capability is hidden or unknown, so the correct answer is a refusal, novel identity – new names, aliases or descriptions, or an added device of the same type, new home – 20 new homes with new rooms and device types, new vocabulary – another ecosystem’s command grammar like Home Assistant-style service calls, vendor-prefixed methods, REST requests, or HomeBench’s format with synonym operation names, e.g., set_level for set_brightness, rendering – the same home in other formats like JSON, YAML, shuffled rooms, etc., registry scale – homes enlarged to about 300, 600 or 1,000 operations while keeping the existing request, and state dependence – a change by a stated amount that stays in range in one state and leaves it in another.

All categories start from an Trek-Base request. 6 categories were generated with GPT-5 (prompts in Appendix 10.4); the remaining 3 were built deterministically (rendering, registry_scale, and state_dependent). Trek-Robust has about 2,000 valid rows: 200 per category, and about 400 for counterfactual (roughly 200 complete pairs).

6.3 Trek-Memory: Conversational Memory Evaluation

Trek-Base and Trek-Robust score each request on its own. To test memory across turns, we build the Trek-Memory dataset. It groups the Trek-Base requests into 100 multi-turn conversations, one per home, each with a single user, and adds requests that need memory. Each home’s requests are shuffled once. After each turn, the ground truth actions are applied to the simulated home, so later turns see the updated state. Relative requests (e.g., “turn it up by 2”) are answered from this updated state, including changes made by the added turns. Requests whose correct answer can no longer be determined are dropped.

We add about 30 memory turns to each home, 2,895 in total. They are built from templates and each home’s devices:

  • Preferences. We assign two preferences to each of the 100 homes. The user states the preference (“My usual brightness for the balcony light is 30%”) and later asks for it (“Set the balcony light to my usual brightness”). The first preference tests situation-specific values, explicit-value overrides, and subsequent recall. The second tests using, updating, and forgetting a preference, with a final request requiring refusal.

  • Alias. Two devices per home receive nicknames (e.g., “Bubbles” and “the tall fan”), each used twice. The user then forgets one nickname and reuses it, or uses an undefined nickname, both requiring refusal.

  • Corrections. A request uses a phrase that matches no device. The user then names the intended device (“No, I meant the store room light”), and a later request reuses the phrase for that device.

  • Follow-ups. Twice per home, a request that names a device is followed right away by one that refers to it as “it” or “its”.

Each group of memory turns starts in the first half of the conversation, with a random number of original requests between its turns. We then reword the added turns with GPT-5 (prompt in Appendix 10.5), one call per home, so they do not all share the template wording. Rewording changes only the text; ground truth answers and turn order stay the same. Memory has 14,906 turns turns across 100 conversations, with a median of 182 turns per conversation.

7 Evaluation

We evaluate Trail on the following research questions:

  1. 1.

    How accurate is Trail, and how robust is it to variations in homes and request phrasing (§7.1)?

  2. 2.

    How efficient is Trail in terms of latency (§7.2)?

  3. 3.

    How well does Trail generalise to unseen homes (§7.3)?

  4. 4.

    Can Trail leverage conversational memory and state across multiple turns (§7.4)?

Baselines. We compare Trail against Qwen3.5-4B (i.e. JevK5’s decision engine) with prompting and finetuning on approximately 22,000 adapted HomeBench requests, VCU-LLM Zhang et al. (2026), Sasha King et al. (2024), AdaHome Lim et al. (2026), and Domux iFLYTEK Open Source (2026). VCU-LLM uses a finetuned Llama-3.2-1B with a 119-request retrieval bank, a hand-written verb dictionary, and a validation-tuned retrieval threshold. Sasha and AdaHome use Qwen3.5-4B. We use Domux’s released weights and reproduce VCU-LLM, Sasha, and AdaHome from their papers, reusing available prompts and mapping Domux’s predicted slots to the home’s registry. Qwen3.5-4B uses the prompt from HomeBench Li et al. (2025). The prompts can be found in Appendix 10.6.

Metrics. We report strict exact match accuracy: a request is correct only if the multiset of actions a system outputs equals the ground truth, where each item is a complete device call or a refusal (error_input); a request with several sub-commands is correct only if every one is. This strict criterion reflects the need for reliable smart home control, where even a single incorrect sub-command can leave the user’s request partially unfulfilled or cause unintended changes to the home.

7.1 Accuracy and Robustness

Trail trades some accuracy on familiar requests for greater robustness to variations in homes. Table 2 reports the accuracy of Trail and the baselines on Trek-Base and Trek-Robust. On Trek-Base, finetuned Qwen3.5-4B achieves the highest accuracy at 89.7%, followed by Trail at 86.2%. However, in Trek-Robust, the finetuned generator drops by 19.9 percentage points to 69.8%, while Trail drops by only 0.9 points, making 2.1×\times fewer errors. Although both Trailand Qwen3.5-4B are fine-tuned, they learn different capabilities. Qwen3.5-4B learns to map requests directly to device calls, performing well on familiar homes and phrasing. In contrast, Trailselects rooms, devices, and operations from the current home’s registry, including refusal when appropriate. This makes Trailmore robust to changes in homes and requests, as tested by Trek-Robust.

Accuracy by Request Wording. Trail reliably handles explicit commands but loses accuracy as phrasing becomes more colloquial or intent less specified, like most baselines. Table 3 shows Trail dropping from 99.4% on original requests to 88.5% on colloquial, 81.7% on implied-device, and 70.3% on goal-only requests. Finetuned Qwen3.5-4B outperforms Trail across all styles, while VCU-LLM achieves the highest goal-only accuracy (79.5%).

Robustness Across Trek-Robust Categories. Trail outperforms the baselines on most categories in Trek-Robust, especially when actions depend on runtime device state, capability information, and API vocabulary, while also achieving the highest accuracy on new homes and unseen capabilities. Table 4 presents the per-category results on Trek-Robust. For state-dependent requests (SD), Trail achieves 0.995 accuracy by computing the result directly from device state, whereas the strongest baseline reaches only 0.475. When capability information is missing or unknown (MI), the correct response is a refusal. Trail correctly refuses 0.885 of these requests, substantially outperforming Sasha (0.630) and Domux (0.690). When the API vocabulary changes (NV), Trail and VCU-LLM maintain high accuracy (0.915 and 0.875) by selecting operations from the runtime registry, while the finetuned generator, trained to produce HomeBench-style calls, achieves only 0.600. Trail also achieves the highest accuracy on new homes (NH, 0.685) and unseen capabilities (UC, 0.670), although these remain its lowest-scoring categories, indicating that unfamiliar configurations and capabilities are more difficult to handle.

The finetuned generator performs best on registry rendering (Rnd, 0.910) and scale (Scale, 0.950), where the underlying requests and operations remain largely familiar. Counterfactual requests (CF) further highlight this distinction: the same instruction is evaluated under different home configurations that require different outputs. Trail achieves the highest accuracy (0.851), outperforming the finetuned Qwen3.5-4B (0.799). This suggests that the finetuned generator relies more heavily on request-to-action patterns learned during training, whereas Trail better adapts its decisions to changes in the runtime environment.

7.2 Latency

Trail achieves low inference latency despite requiring multiple typed decisions per request, and maintains this advantage when conversational memory is enabled. Fig. 2 plots the end-to-end latency of Trail and its baselines on Trek-Base, Trek-Robust and Trek-Memory (the exact results are in Tables 7, 8 and 9 in the Appendix 10.1). For each dataset, every system answers the same requests (500 for Trek-Base and Trek-Robust, 575 i.e. 3 conversations for Trek-Memory), one at a time as a smart home assistant would serve them. All systems run on a single NVIDIA RTX A4500 GPU. Trail runs with Hugging Face Transformers; the LLM baselines run with vLLM, which is heavily optimized.

Trail achieves a median latency of 0.166 s on Trek-Base and 0.169 s on Trek-Robust, making it 3.2×\times and 3.8×\times faster than its competitive baseline, the finetuned Qwen3.5-4B, respectively. This is despite Trail requiring an average of 5.4 and 4.5 typed decisions per request, compared with a single generation call for Qwen3.5-4B. VCU-LLM achieves the lowest median latency (0.079 s on Trek-Base and 0.094 s on Trek-Robust), but its accuracy drops substantially on Trek-Robust (0.505 versus 0.853 for Trail). Domux matches Trail’s median but is far less accurate.

Enabling memory increases Trail’s median latency from 0.172 s to 0.215 s (25%) and the average number of typed decisions from 5.7 to 7.5 per turn. In comparison, providing the full conversation history to finetuned Qwen3.5-4B increases its median latency from 0.486 s to 0.727 s. With memory enabled, Trail remains 3.4×\times faster at the median and 1.6×\times faster at P90 than Qwen3.5-4B with history.

7.3 Generalization

Trail grounds its decisions in the home’s runtime device registry, allowing it to operate on unseen home configurations without home-specific training. To evaluate this, we retrain Trail on 80 homes, excluding all requests from the remaining 20. As Table 5 shows, the model trained on 80 homes achieves nearly identical accuracy on the 20 held-out homes as the model trained on all 100 homes (0.860 versus 0.859). It also performs comparably on Trek-Robust’s new-home category (0.695 versus 0.685), which contains 20 generated homes unseen by both models. These results suggest that Trail learns to select actions from the runtime registry rather than relying on memorized home-specific configurations, enabling generalization to unseen homes without retraining.

7.4 Memory

Structured memory substantially improves Trail’s ability to resolve conversational requests without degrading performance on ordinary requests, outperforming finetuned Qwen3.5-4B even when provided with the full conversation history. Table 6 shows the accuracy on Trek-Memory. Adding memory increases accuracy on memory-dependent turns from 0.277 to 0.756, while accuracy on original Trek-Base requests remains nearly unchanged (0.872 versus 0.870). Providing the full conversation history to finetuned Qwen3.5-4B improves its memory accuracy from 0.350 to 0.425, but it still falls substantially behind Trail (0.756). Although the finetuned generator performs better on original requests (0.898 versus 0.870), Trail achieves higher overall accuracy (0.848 versus 0.809).

8 Related Work

8.1 Natural-Language Smart Home Control

Recent works improve natural-language driven smart home control using model adaptation, retrieval and planning. VCU-LLM Zhang et al. (2026) combines a finetuned Llama3.2-1B SLM with knowledge retrieval and KV cache optimization. MiCU Han et al. (2026) uses curriculum learning, chain of thought reasoning, and reinforcement learning, while Domux iFLYTEK Open Source (2026) finetunes a Gemma-4-E2B SLM to convert user commands into structured, pipe-delimited slots. AdaHome Lim et al. (2026) routes commands to either a direct or a Chain-of-Draft reasoning planner based on the request complexity.

Other smart home control systems emphasize goal interpretation and tool orchestration. SAGE Rivkin et al. (2024) grounds user requests in smart home actions through LLM-driven tool use such as: device disambiguation, API inspection, preference retrieval, and device command execution. Similarly, Sasha King et al. (2024) uses an iterative reasoning process to produce action plans to respond to vague user commands.

These systems establish the value of domain specific training and context for smart home interaction. Trail focuses on a different inference mechanism: composing typed candidate decisions over a runtime-constructed device hierarchy rather than generating complete commands or action plans.

8.2 Grounded Action Selection and Hierarchical Predictions

Grounding language in executable behavior extends beyond smart home control. SayCan Ahn et al. (2022) extracts and leverages the knowledge within LLMs in physically-grounded tasks to select robot actions. ReAct Yao et al. (2023) interleaves reasoning, actions, and knowledge based or environmental observations. Hierarchical structured prediction also has established precedence in Abstract Syntax Networks Rabinovich et al. (2017), that decode code generation tasks using syntax tree structures.

Trail applies both these ideas to a runtime-defined smart home action space: its hierarchy exposes room, device, operation, and parameter decisions to a pretrained typed decision engine. Its contribution is its architecture, rather than hierarchical prediction or grounded action selection in isolation.

8.3 Constrained Language-Model Inference

Constrained decoding restricts generated outputs during inference. XGrammar Dong et al. (2024) provides a flexible and efficient structure generation engine for LLMs. Synchromesh Poesia et al. (2022) allows enforcing syntactic and semantic constraints on the LLM output. SGLang Zheng et al. (2024) provides structured program execution and candidate selection.

Trail is a domain-specific orchestration framework rather than a general language-model runtime. It explores the benefit of exposing smart home structure directly through hierarchical typed decisions.

9 Conclusion

Trail reformulates smart home control as hierarchical typed decisions over a smart home’s actions instead of open-ended device call generation. By restricting selections to valid candidates and abstaining when confidence is low, Trail avoids unsupported actions and reduces incorrect executions. Its structured memory further enables personalized, multi-turn interactions without including conversation history in the model’s prompt. To evaluate Trail, we introduce 3 datasets extended from HomeBench Li et al. (2025): Trek-Base, Trek-Robust and Trek-Memory. Trail achieves 85.3% accuracy on Trek-Robust versus 69.8% for a finetuned Qwen3.5-4B baseline, while remaining competitive on Trek-Base requests. With memory, Trail resolves 75.6% of the memory requests, compared with 42.5% for the finetuned baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of hierarchical typed decisions for local smart home control.
